title: The House Built to Burn
hookLine: Yudhishthira walks into a fine new house, smells ghee and lac, and knows
carry: anumana: a real sign, and a rule that holds
tomorrow: can you prove God exists, step by step?

cards: In the Mahabharata, the five Pandava brothers and their mother are sent off to the town of Varanavata, and lodged in a fine new house. Their cousin Duryodhana had it built.
Before they left, their wise uncle Vidura warned Yudhishthira, in a coded riddle, about fire. Now Yudhishthira walks through the door and stops. He smells ghee.
He smells fat. He smells lac, the resin that burns fast. He turns to Bhima and says quietly: this house was made to burn.

teach.h: ANUMANA: FROM A SIGN TO THE UNSEEN.
teach.b: No flame, no confession, and still Yudhishthira knew. Nyaya has a word for that leap: anumana, inference, knowing something you can't see by way of a sign you can.
Nyaya teachers lay it out with their classic case: the hill has fire, because it has smoke.

teach.h: SMOKE ON THE HILL, FIRE BEHIND.
teach.b: It works because smoke and fire have been seen together again and again, at the kitchen hearth; and where there's no fire, like a still lake, there's no smoke.
Later Nyaya teachers named that rule vyapti, pervasion: wherever there's smoke, there's fire. With a real sign and a rule that holds, the leap isn't a guess. It's knowing.

teach.h: HE SMELLED IT, AND VIDURA AGREED.
teach.b: The sign was real: he didn't trust a glance; he smelled it, ghee and fat and lac. The rule held: a house made of what burns fastest is made to burn.
And a second means of knowing agreed: Vidura's warning, the word of someone reliable. But Nyaya cares just as much how a leap goes wrong.
One trap: the sign isn't what you think; a gray haze might be mist, not smoke. Another: the rule run backward. Wherever there's fire, there's smoke?

A red-hot iron ball glows with fire and gives off none. And notice, the brothers didn't panic. A digger sent by Vidura made them a tunnel, and on the night the house went up, they slipped away through it.
Nyaya doesn't ask you to stop inferring.

teach.h: IS THE SIGN REAL? DOES THE RULE HOLD?
teach.b: It asks two questions first, and they work at home too: is the sign real, and does the rule really run this way?

how: In traditional Sanskrit study, students of Nyaya learn inference through the example of smoke and fire on a hill, practicing how to state a sign, a rule and a supporting case, and how to spot reasons that only look like reasons.

o: a school that treats knowing as whatever most people agree on
a school of logic that checks the leap from sign to unseen
a school whose rule says all fire must give off smoke

games.q: smoke on the hill — tap the pairs.
p: inference: from a sign to the unseen
a sign that only looks like smoke

s: in Nyaya, inference is just an educated guess
with a real sign and a rule that holds, the leap from the sign to the unseen is knowing.
wherever there is fire, there is smoke
a red-hot iron ball has fire and no smoke. the rule runs only one way.
Yudhishthira only learned the house was a trap once it caught fire
he smelled ghee, fat and lac on arrival, and Vidura's warning agreed with the sign.

games.q: you're a Nyaya student on a ridge. a gray haze is rising behind the next hill. before you say fire, what do you check?
o: whether it's really smoke, and not mist or dust.
whether your friends agree with you.
games.why: the first trap is a sign that isn't what you think. same color, no fire. before you reason from smoke, make sure it's smoke.

practice: Bring to mind a conclusion you reached this week about someone from a sign, a look, a silence, a tone of voice, and ask: was it really what I took it for, or could it have been mist?
Then ask whether you know this sign always comes with that meaning. Don't decide anything; just let the leap slow down until you can see it, and if you pray, ask the God you know for clear eyes.

wordCard.voice: Nyaya. Today, anumana, inference: Yudhishthira smelled lac and knew, because the sign was real and the rule held.

orig.note: Sanskrit: anumana, inference, one of Nyaya's means of knowing.

carryVoice: Your line: anumana, a real sign, and a rule that holds. Is it smoke, or is it mist? See you tomorrow.
